question: Can the optimal-hyperplane method be extended to non-separable data and combined with kernel dot-products to give a high-generalisation classifier for two-group problems such as digit recognition?
hypothesis: Because the bound on test error depends on the number of support vectors rather than the feature-space dimension, high-degree polynomial support-vector networks should generalise well in very high-dimensional feature spaces.
contributions: Soft-margin hyperplane for training data that cannot be separated without error
Support-vector network: optimal/soft-margin hyperplane combined with a kernel (convolution of the dot-product)
Experiments on USPS and NIST digits compared against classical learners

method.summary: Soft-margin optimal hyperplanes solved as a dual quadratic program with polynomial kernel (u.v+1)^d; ten one-vs-rest separators per digit problem, prediction by maximum output. Tested on USPS (degrees 1 to 7) and NIST (degree 4).
method.task: handwritten digit classification (10 classes via 10 binary separators)

datasets.name: US Postal Service (USPS) digits
datasets.size: 7,300 training and 2,000 test patterns, 16 x 16 pixels (256 inputs)
datasets.preprocessing: centering, de-slanting and smoothing; Gaussian smoothing kernel with standard deviation 0.75

datasets.name: NIST (Special Database 3)
datasets.size: 60,000 training and 10,000 test patterns, 28 x 28 (784 inputs)
datasets.split: 60,000 / 10,000, a 50-50 mixture of the NIST training and test sets

models.name: Support-vector network, polynomial kernel
models.architecture: soft-margin SVM, K(u,v)=(u.v+1)^d, ten binary separators, maximum output

models.name: Linear classifier, k=3 nearest neighbour (60,000 prototypes), LeNet1, LeNet4
models.architecture: NIST benchmark entries from Bottou et al. 1994

models.name: Human, CART, C4.5, best 2-layer NN, LeNet1 (USPS)
models.architecture: collected from publications and own experiments

training.objective: minimise (1/2) w.w + C F(sum xi_i^sigma) with sigma = 1, F(u)=u^2, subject to y_i(w.x_i+b) >= 1 - xi_i, xi_i >= 0; solved as the dual quadratic program in (A, delta)
training.optimizer: quadratic programming on the dual; incremental scheme over data portions described in Section 2
training.regularisation: margin maximisation; C trades complexity against training error

other.C: value never reported; no C sweep or model selection described
other.time: training time claimed to depend on number of support vectors, not degree; no timings given

inference.samples: single run per setting; no seeds or error bars

metrics.name: Test error (combined classifier)
metrics.definition: error of the maximum-output combination of ten classifiers (NIST)

eval.protocol: Single train/test split per database; NIST comparison is the Bottou et al. 1994 benchmark run over 2 weeks; authors contributed only the SVM entry.

results.claim: Ten degree-4 polynomial SVMs combined reach 1.1% test error on the NIST benchmark.
results.setup: NIST 60,000 train / 10,000 test, degree-4 polynomial, no pre-processing, ten separators, maximum output. Ties LeNet4 per Fig 9 (bar heights not in text).
results.quote: The combined performance of the ten classifiers on the test set is 1.1% error.

results.claim: On USPS the degree-1 polynomial has 12.0% raw error and degree 2 has 4.7%.
results.setup: USPS, 256 inputs, pre-processed; training data not linearly separable.
results.table: Table 2, row degree 1, column Raw error

results.claim: Feature-space dimension grows from about 33000 (degree 2) to about 1 x 10^16 (degree 7) while raw error stays 4.2 to 4.7%; support vectors rise only from 127 to 190.
results.table: Table 2, row degree 7, column Support vectors

results.claim: USPS baselines: human 2.5, CART 17, C4.5 16, best 2-layer NN 6.6, LeNet1 5.1 (raw error %); SVMs of degree 2 or higher beat LeNet1.

results.claim: The observed support-vector ratio bounds single-classifier error at no more than 3% against actual test error no more than 1.5%.
results.setup: USPS, observed SV counts used in place of expectations in bound (5).
results.quote: In all cases the upper bound on the error probability for the single classifier does not exceed 3% (on the test data the actual error does not exceed 1.5% for the single classifier).

results.claim: NIST degree-4 separators commit training errors: average 0.02%, about 12 per class.
results.setup: NIST, degree 4, per classifier; SVs per classifier 989 to 2765 (Table 3).
results.quote: The average frequency of training errors is 0.02% ~ 12 per class.

results.claim: Degree-1 USPS classifier averages 34 training misclassifications per classifier; degree 2 has 4 in total.
results.quote: the number ofmis-classifications on the training set averages to 34 per classifier for the linear case.

results.claim: The SV expected-error bound ratio can be as low as 0.03 on a real problem.
results.setup: Stated in the introduction; bound is for separable training data.

results.claim: The SVM does not use image geometry; per Bottou et al., it would do as well with permuted pixels.
results.quote: In fact the classifier would do as weil if the image pixels were encrypted e.g. by a fixed, random permutation.

results.quote: For the experiments reported in this paper we used k = 2 and solved the quadratic programming problem (51).

limits: Polynomial kernels only; RBF mentioned as implementable (s5.2) but no RBF result.
No value of C, no C sweep or cross-validation reported.
Squared penalty (k = 2) used in experiments; the linear F(u)=u case is derived but not tested.
Support vectors defined by equality on the margin; non-zero slack vectors counted separately (USPS 200 for degree 1).
Single runs, no error bars; no training times given despite the speed claim.
Two-group classifier; multiclass by one separator per class with maximum output.
Sigma = 1 chosen to avoid NP-completeness, not minimising the training error count.
